summary: Turns trial done as a stand-alone numpy voxel job under out/r14/turns/ (nothing in src/ touched, no build, no publishing). Result is disappointing and clear: "both rules at every step" does NOT give a 3D Julia set with fine detail in every direction that stays whole off the x-axis. The union set (bounded for some order) is whole and seam-free off the axis but swells into a fat lump that swallows the flat set; the common set (bounded for every order) is EMPTY for every c tried off the x-axis. Only for c on the x-axis (c = -1) is there something to look at: the union of the exact rule (E) is the basilica solid with beads round both circles plus smaller warts between them, with no seam. Verdict: none of the four is worth building as a general approach; E-union could be shown as a curiosity for c on the x-axis only (the same limit the paper states), and it would need a new voxel-texture drawing path, not a normal approach entry. Method: because both rules square the length, the set for ALL orders at any depth can be computed exactly (to grid resolution) by a pull-back on one grid, so Julia sets were run to convergence (depth 19 to 46), not just 8 to 12 steps; Mandelbrot solids were brute-forced over every order to depth 12. Time used: about 70 minutes.

findings: Is the set whole for c off the x-axis (no tear)? Union: yes. E-union is one single piece at all three off-axis c (measured, grid 257) and shows no seam by eye; K-union is one main piece holding 99.9 percent or more with a few loose crumbs (25 and 11 pieces at the two off-plane c, 1 for the rabbit). Common: there is nothing to be whole: it is empty (0 voxels) for every c off the x-axis, for both E and K.

Beads round two circles for c = -1? E-union: yes and more. Looking along the x-axis there are four large beads up, down, left and right (both circles), and between them a net of smaller warts over the whole ball, with no crease (the lab's 'two planes' entry shows creases there). E-common has no beads at all: a smooth basilica. One rule alone has beads on one circle only. Seen by eye, not measured.

Fat blob, dust, or fine structure? Off the axis the union is a fat lump: volume 2.0 to 5.5 against 0.9 at c = -1 (E: 2.02, 4.55, 4.80; K: 1.14, 5.50, 4.06). E's lump is smooth with a few knobs, K's is lumpier with pits. The common set is nothing. Only at c = -1 is there bead detail (E-union). No variant gives fine detail in every direction off the axis.

Slice at z = 0 against the flat Julia set, c = -1, pair E (measured, grid 257): union is a little bigger (area 1.65 against 1.41, 1348 extra pixels, 24 missing of 8083); common is smaller (1.29, 720 flat pixels missing: the top and bottom buds and the fringe). Rabbit, E: union is far bigger (4.24 against 1.31) and holds the whole flat rabbit inside a lump; common is empty. So neither keeps the flat set as its cut.

How K differs from E: K is worse on every count. Its one-rule cut is already not the flat set (3012 of 8083 flat pixels missing at c = -1, as the brief expected: a cousin). Its solids are lopsided (no mirror symmetry x to -x), smaller (union 0.42 against 0.89 at c = -1), and the union sheds loose crumbs (133 pieces at c = -1, 25 over 20 voxels). Off the axis it behaves like E: union a lump, common empty.

Mandelbrot solids (depth 12, grid 161): union is a big craggy lump four to five times the one-rule solid (2.10 against 0.46 for E) whose cut at z = 0 swallows the flat Mandelbrot set (3.22 against 1.92, nothing of the flat set missing); common is a small smooth tadpole (0.21), a teardrop with a needle along the x-axis, whose cut keeps only the core of the flat set (0.55 of 1.92). Neither cut is the flat Mandelbrot set.

Why (reasoned, not measured): a free choice between two rules at every step is a lot of freedom. For 'some order' there is nearly always a mix that steers the orbit back, so the set swells. For 'every order' one bad mix is enough to throw a point out, and off the axis there always is one. On the x-axis the two rules agree along the axis itself, which is why both sets survive there. This matches the paper's own limit (second construction only for c real).

Cost per picture point (measured counts): the plain way needs about 90 to 160 rule evaluations for a point just outside the set and 1800 (depth 10) to 6900 (depth 12) for a point inside, against 10 to 12 for one rule, and there is no distance estimate, so the lab's ray marcher could not use its usual shortcut. The grid way costs 2 evaluations per voxel once, then the solid is a 3D table: cheap to draw but detail stops at the grid (no deep zoom).

VERDICT: none of the four gives what the user hoped for, and I would not build any of them as a general approach. K-union, K-common and E-common have nothing to offer (lopsided, crumbs, smooth, or empty). The only one with something to see is E-union, and only for c on the x-axis: a seam-free basilica with beads in every direction. If it is wanted as a curiosity it must be labelled 'c on the x-axis only', and it would cost a new drawing path in the lab (compute a 3D table by pull-back, about 30 passes over a grid, then march that table), not a normal entry with mul/pw/sqr; I estimate that as a round of its own. Only c = -1 was tried on the axis.

findings: quat4, plain words: With the dials at 0 the picture is the Lathe's, ring for ring (pixel for pixel in two pictures). Moving the slice gives a smaller solid of rings, tilting it to 90 gives a plain ball, and the Julia sets are the classic quaternion shapes, smooth sheets like pulled taffy. The slice at z = 0 is the flat set only with all three dials at 0. It brings other slices of the same family, and no finer detail than the Lathe already shows.

rotor, plain words: It is the Lathe's solid turned so that its rings go round the reference axis; with the recipe's own z-axis it looks like a spinning top standing upright. The slice at z = 0 is the flat set only with the axis along x (with the axis elsewhere in the flat plane it is the flat set turned by the longitude; with the z-axis it is a disc with thin circles). It brings nothing the Lathe does not have: measured for five axes, no exception. The image's recipe is the quaternion square.

rotorframe, plain words: A swirled body of smooth layered sheets, wound like a shell, with no fine bumps; the Julia set for c = -1 carries a large flat half-disc wall, as wide as the whole set, where half of the plane y = 0 is crushed. The slice at z = 0 is exactly the flat set (0 of 6,000 points differ). It is a rule the list did not have (33 degrees from the Lathe's answer on average, 39 from the Mandelbulb's), but it tears at the z-axis, crushes a half-plane and turns about 13 % of directions over, and the look is the same smooth-sheet family as the quaternion entries.

kleinsq, plain words: The Mandelbrot solid is one lumpy, creased body with a spike, much like 'Sphere inversions, one plane'; the Julia set for c = -1 is a chain of bodies along the x-axis with small buds; the rabbit is one angular lump; for c off the flat plane it falls into shards. The slice at z = 0 is NOT the flat set: it is an angular cousin (about 80 % of the flat Mandelbrot set is inside it, about an eighth of it is outside). What it brings is the paper's road made visible; as a picture it is not better than the one-plane entry, and it loses the exact slice.

kleinsq2, plain words: For c = -1 the Julia set is a chain of bodies with buds round two circles, above and below as well as left and right: the look of 'Sphere inversions, two planes', with rougher, knobbly buds. For the Mandelbrot solid, the rabbit and c = (-1, 0.15, 0.1) it is a mass of shards. The slices at z = 0 and y = 0 are the same cousin as kleinsq's, not the flat set. It brings nothing the two-planes entry does not have, and has the same limit the paper states (c on the x-axis only).

Where my numbers differ from the section's 'expected': kleinsq agrees with z^n at 2(n + 1) directions on the equator, not n + 1: the points where the caps touch and also the cap centres (n = 2: every 60 degrees; n = 3: every 45; n = 4: every 36). The page says 'six directions, 60 degrees apart' for n = 2.

Everything else the section expected was confirmed: quat4 = Lathe at 0, rings for w not 0, shells at tilt 90; rotor = Lathe turned, for every axis tried; rotorframe exact on z = 0 and on the half-plane y = 0, x > 0, torn at the z-axis; kleinsq2 jumps on the planes |y| = |z| (up to 180 degrees).

Found beyond the section: rotorframe at n = 2 crushes the whole half-plane y = 0, x < 0 onto the positive x-axis, has no jump across that half-plane at whole powers, and turns 13 to 14 % of directions over (mostly near the poles). In kleinsq a quarter of all directions (the two patches round the poles no cap covers) is only mirrored at n = 2, 42 % at n = 3, 52 % at n = 4.

Smoke test cause, measured on a fresh page (out/r14/rules/twins.log): 408 pick probes of lathe and quat4 differ in 0 places in Mandelbrot mode and 0 in Julia c = -1; axisbulb and quat4 differ in 0 in Julia c = -1 (5 in Mandelbrot mode). So the smoke's 'no two entries draw the same picture' rule must allow quat4 with lathe (both modes) and quat4 with axisbulb (Julia).

rotor at latitude 90 uses a reference axis snapped to exactly (0, 0, 1) in both shader and MATH (values under 1e-6 are set to 0); within 0.00003 degree of 90 the axis is therefore not moved.

kleinsq and kleinsq2 at powers that are not whole numbers >= 2 follow the section literally: caps of the nearest whole power >= 2, length by the real power. For these two entries mul(v, v) is not v^2 (mul is the one-plane product, as the section asked), so a typed formula 'z*z + c' differs from 'z^2 + c' if the formula compiler does not turn it into sqr.

The merged page was not tested by me. With the rules engineer's 15 or more entries the smoke step that compares pictures pair by pair, and the step that checks each entry's explanation (it needs a non-empty name, tag, formula and about for every entry), may fail for reasons in their file.

The verdict notes of the new entries are no longer permanently on show under the dials; they appear on hover and under About this approach. If the user expects to see an entry's honest verdict without asking for it, that is a regression against the page rule that every entry says where it falls short.
The user may miss the old reset that put every approach's dials back at once; only Reset everything does that now.

On a phone with the picture pinned the open list has room for about 5 rows at a time on a real touch screen (reasoned, not measured), so a list of 15 or more entries means a good deal of thumb scrolling inside the list.

Opening the menu scrolls the controls column so that the list fits the window (about 290 px from the top of the page at 1400x950). The picture stays in place on a wide window, but the jump of the column may surprise.
Collapse all and Expand all now treat approach and equation as one section, and the page has one section fewer; any outside script that looked for a details element with id secEq will find a div.
